doc.title: Houston Person Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 2, 1998 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Always a musician: leading his own band, hustling and early money
summary: Person says he never held a non-music job, only sidemanned with Johnny Hammond Smith for two years, then hustled for his own band with low pay and Prestige's support.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: After you got out of the service did you ever work non-musical jobs?
You’ve been able to pretty much do it in music?
And you started almost from the beginning having your own band.
Yeah. I didn’t work with any groups except I went with Johnny Hammond Smith’s for about two years. And that was it. So I didn’t have any — there was nothing visual.
Nobody knew who I was. And I just stuck it out. But if you get a wife, four girls to feed and a mortgage, you’ll find a way. That’s what happened.
I had to keep myself saying now I want to play music. I’ve got to make this work. I’ve got to. So I got out and hustled.
Hustling meant going to different clubs and getting your band booked in there—
I mean what kind of money would you have been making with your band — if you don’t mind me getting personal — like in the early years?

When I first started I realized that. I know the economics of jazz so I gave people offers they couldn’t refuse to get in the door. And just kept building and building and building. And I was with Prestige Records and they were good to me, they stuck with me for a while and let me get my feet out there. And I had a lot of help on the way, a lot of people helped me. So that was really — and there are some good people in jazz. There are some cut throats, but hey, it’s all fair, it balances out.
But even the cut throats are nice. And you’ve got your jazz characters, they’ll always be there.
